name: Passionflower / chamomile tea
lead: Passionflower and chamomile tea is a bedtime herbal infusion that people drink to wind down and sleep better. In appearance and physique communities the point is sleep: people who want clearer-looking skin, less tired eyes and better recovery from training treat good sleep as part of looking their best, and a calming tea is one of the routines used to get there. Chamomile tea is made from the dried flowers of German or Roman chamomile [1], and passionflower (Passiflora incarnata, or maypop) is a plant whose dried aerial parts are listed in the European and British Pharmacopoeias [2].

Research on the two herbs is uneven. A 2011 double-blind crossover study in 41 healthy adults found sleep quality rated significantly better after a week of passionflower tea than after placebo, which the authors described as initial evidence of short-term subjective benefit [3]. A 2020 randomised trial in adults with insomnia disorder reported significantly longer total sleep time with a passionflower extract than placebo on polysomnography, while other measures improved over time without differing from placebo [4]. A systematic review of nine passionflower trials covering stress, anxiety and sleep reported generally favourable effects over trials lasting one to 30 days [5].

Wikipedia states that there is no clinical evidence that chamomile treats any disease, that its anti-anxiety potential is under preliminary research, and that there is no good evidence for insomnia [1]. Reviews of herbal sleep aids describe interactions with the GABA system as a proposed route for sedative effects [6].
infobox: Chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla or Chamaemelum nobile); Passiflora incarnata

paras: Chamomile flowers contain flavonoids and polyphenols including apigenin, quercetin and luteolin [1]. Passionflower contains flavonoids such as chrysin, apigenin, luteolin and quercetin, plus alkaloids, with the highest flavonoid concentration in the leaves [2].

Chamomile's main compound classes are coumarins, flavonoids and polyphenols, with apigenin, quercetin, patuletin, luteolin and daphnin among those named, plus essential-oil components such as farnesol and nerolidol [1]. A clinical pharmacokinetic study characterised the absorption, distribution, metabolism and excretion of apigenin and its glycosides in healthy men [15]. A review of chamomile tea's bioactivity summarises its reported antioxidant, anti-inflammatory and sedative actions in laboratory and clinical work [16].

The word chamomile comes from the Greek for 'earth apple', and the spelling is recorded in English from the 13th century; Nicholas Culpeper's 17th-century Complete Herbal includes entries on it, and the flowers were historically used to flavour beer [1]. Two species are most often used for tea: Matricaria chamomilla, called German chamomile, and Chamaemelum nobile, called Roman or English chamomile [1]. Chamomile is also used to flavour foods, mouthwash, soaps and cosmetics [1].
Passionflower, Passiflora incarnata or maypop, is a vine whose dried aerial parts are listed in the European and British Pharmacopoeias and are used in herbal teas, tinctures and capsules [2].

Chamomile and passionflower are sold as single-herb teas and as blends, often alongside lemon balm or valerian. On T Nation, lifters describe alternating chamomile and passionflower tea at night, adding passionflower tea before bed, or taking tea with melatonin as part of a wind-down routine [7][8][9]. One lifter says passionflower extract takes the edge off without the melatonin 'hangover' [10]. Another notes the routine itself, not only the herbs, may be what helps [11].

Reviews of herbal sleep remedies list valerian, passionflower, lemon balm, lavender and Californian poppy among centuries-old herbal treatments reported to reduce sleep latency, and attribute their sedative action to interactions with GABA receptors [6]. A 2004 clinical evaluation looked at the activity of passionflower dry-extract capsules [17].

A double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study of 41 healthy adults found that passionflower tea gave significantly better sleep-quality ratings than placebo, with polysomnography in ten participants [3].

In adults with insomnia disorder, a double-blind placebo-controlled study of Passiflora incarnata reported a significant increase in total sleep time versus placebo (P = 0.049); sleep efficiency and wake after sleep onset improved within the group but did not differ from placebo [4].

A pilot double-blind trial in 36 outpatients with generalised anxiety compared passionflower extract with oxazepam over four weeks and found no significant difference, with less job-performance impairment on passionflower [12]. A 2020 systematic review of nine passionflower trials and a 2022 network meta-analysis of medicinal herbs for anxiety are further sources [5][13]. A registered phase 1 trial (2019, 27 participants) tested a herbal formula, Rest-ZZZ, in healthy adults with difficulty sleeping [14].

For chamomile, Wikipedia cites a 2015 systematic review and meta-analysis by Leach and Page that found no good evidence that herbal medicines including chamomile are useful for insomnia, and a 2011 review by Sarris and colleagues that put chamomile's anti-anxiety potential under preliminary research [1]. A double-blind trial also tested passionflower in opiate withdrawal [18]. A review of anxiety, depression and insomnia in primary care covers herbal options among treatments [19].

Chamomile may interact with some herbs and drugs, may worsen pollen allergies, and can cause reactions in people allergic to daisies, ragweed and related plants; Roman chamomile may cause uterine contractions and is advised against in pregnancy [1]. Passionflower may increase the effect of sedatives, anticoagulants and MAO inhibitors, and pregnant or breastfeeding women are advised to consult a professional [2].

Wikipedia adds that chamomile is not recommended with anticoagulants because it contains coumarin compounds, although its effect on coagulation is unstudied, and that people with hormone-sensitive conditions are advised to avoid it [1]. A systematic review of food, herbal and supplement interactions with warfarin lists herbal products among agents reported to interact with the anticoagulant [20].

lore.intro: Chamomile and passionflower tea come up in strength-training forums as non-drug options for winding down before bed.

claims.claim: Passionflower tea or extract helps you fall asleep without the melatonin 'hangover'.
claims.believers: Lifters report that passionflower takes the edge off and avoids grogginess [10]; others alternate it with chamomile [8].
claims.experts: A crossover trial found better subjective sleep after passionflower tea in healthy adults [3], and a trial in insomnia reported longer total sleep time [4].

claims.believers: Forum members mention chamomile tea as a go-to wind-down drink [7][9].
claims.experts: Wikipedia states there is no good evidence chamomile treats insomnia and that anti-anxiety effects are under preliminary research [1].

claims.claim: The ritual of a warm drink matters as much as the herbs.
claims.believers: A poster notes it might not be the herbs but a staple routine around winding down [11].
claims.experts: No trial has separated ritual effects from herb effects.

claims.claim: A blend of chamomile, passionflower and valerian is a stronger wind-down than either alone
claims.believers: A poster lists chamomile, passionflower and valerian or licorice blends among sleep aids, adding that the routine itself might be what matters [11]; another user combined passionflower tea with melatonin and ZMA [21].
claims.experts: Reviews describe GABA-system interactions for several of these herbs [6], and trials exist for passionflower alone [3][4]; no trial of such blends in healthy lifters was found.

card.summary: A traditional bedtime herbal tea; popular for relaxation, with little trial evidence for sleep.
card.note: Can trigger allergies in people sensitive to daisy-family plants.

quick.overview:
These are herbal teas drunk at night for relaxation. Chamomile is the more widely known; passionflower is often blended in.
Encyclopedic sources say there is no good clinical evidence for sleep benefits, though the teas are widely used traditionally.
quick.mechanism: Both plants contain flavonoids such as apigenin, which proponents link to calming effects; this has not been established in human trials.
quick.risks: Chamomile can cause allergic reactions and may interact with some drugs; passionflower may add to sedatives and anticoagulants. Pregnancy use is generally flagged for medical advice.

angle.goal: Skin, eyes and recovery via sleep
chain: Warm calming tea as a pre-sleep routine
More rested look, skin recovery and training recovery
angle.text: People drink the tea in the evening to fall asleep more easily. Better sleep is associated by proponents with fresher skin, less under-eye tiredness and better recovery between workouts.
